name: Virtue Ethics
one_line_summary: Ethics centered on character traits and human flourishing rather than rules or consequences.
extended_summary: Virtue Ethics centers moral inquiry on character — on what kind of person one should become — rather than on action-evaluating principles (Deontology) or outcome-evaluating calculations (Consequentialism). The tradition's foundational text is Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, which articulates eudaimonia (human flourishing or the good life) as the proper end of human action and the virtues (excellences of character — courage, temperance, justice, practical wisdom or phronesis, and others) as the stable dispositions through which a flourishing life is constituted. After dominating Western moral philosophy through medieval Christianity (Aquinas's Christianized Aristotelianism), virtue ethics receded under Enlightenment-era enthusiasm for principle-based ethics, and was substantially revived in the 20th century by Elizabeth Anscombe's 1958 'Modern Moral Philosophy', Alasdair MacIntyre's After Virtue (1981), Philippa Foot's Natural Goodness (2001), and Rosalind Hursthouse's On Virtue Ethics (1999). The framework remains a major contemporary normative tradition alongside Deontology and Consequentialism, with applications including professional ethics, virtue epistemology, and political theory.
originators: Aristotle (Nicomachean Ethics); Plato as antecedent; Thomas Aquinas (Christian synthesis); 20th-century revival by Elizabeth Anscombe, Philippa Foot, Alasdair MacIntyre, Rosalind Hursthouse, Martha Nussbaum
year_or_decade: 4th century BCE (Aristotle); 1958 (Anscombe revival); 1981 (MacIntyre After Virtue)
core_components: Eudaimonia (human flourishing) as ethical end; Virtues as stable character dispositions; Phronesis (practical wisdom) as integrating capacity; Doctrine of the mean (virtue as between excess and deficiency); Distinction from rule-based and outcome-based ethics; Habituation as moral education; Tradition-bearing communities (MacIntyre); Care ethics as related contemporary tradition
primary_use_case: Normative ethical theory in academic philosophy; professional ethics (medicine, law, business); foundation for virtue epistemology; influence on positive psychology and character-strengths research; applied ethics including bioethics and business ethics; political philosophy (especially MacIntyre's communitarian critique).
common_criticisms: Action-guidance objection: virtue ethics tells you what kind of person to be but not what to do in specific cases; cultural variability of virtue lists raises relativist concerns; Aristotle's specific virtue list reflects Greek aristocratic culture and excludes major moral concerns (women, slaves, animals); 'doctrine of the mean' resists precise specification; situationist critique (Doris, Harman) from social psychology argues that empirical evidence on cross-situational consistency of personality traits undercuts virtue ethics' character-trait foundations — though virtue ethicists have responded substantively; risks circularity (the virtuous person does the right thing because they are virtuous).
primary_sources: Aristotle. Nicomachean Ethics; Anscombe, G.E.M. (1958). 'Modern Moral Philosophy', Philosophy; MacIntyre, A. (1981). After Virtue; Hursthouse, R. (1999). On Virtue Ethics

name: Deontology
one_line_summary: Ethics grounded in duty and universalizable maxims, independent of consequences.
extended_summary: Deontology (from Greek deon, 'duty') is the family of normative ethical theories holding that the moral status of an action is determined by features intrinsic to the action itself — particularly its conformity to duty, principle, or right — rather than by its consequences. The dominant articulation is Immanuel Kant's, presented in the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785) and Critique of Practical Reason (1788), grounded in the Categorical Imperative with three principal formulations: act only on maxims you could will to be universal laws (Universal Law); treat humanity, in yourself and others, always as an end and never merely as a means (Humanity); and act as if legislating universal laws for a kingdom of ends (Autonomy). Kant's framework grounds duties in pure practical reason, holding that moral worth attaches to acts done from duty rather than from inclination, even when consequences are favorable. Contemporary deontological positions include W.D. Ross's pluralistic prima facie duties, threshold deontology, and Kantian constructivism (Korsgaard, O'Neill). Deontology stands in contrast to consequentialism on the question of whether intrinsic act-features or outcomes are morally fundamental.
originators: Immanuel Kant (foundational); W.D. Ross (pluralistic deontology); contemporary figures including Christine Korsgaard, Onora O'Neill, Frances Kamm
year_or_decade: 1785 (Kant's Groundwork); ongoing tradition through W.D. Ross (1930) and contemporary Kantianism
core_components: Duty as moral foundation; Categorical Imperative (Kant) with three formulations: Universal Law, Humanity (as end not merely means), Autonomy/Kingdom of Ends; Distinction between perfect and imperfect duties; Moral worth from acting from duty rather than inclination; W.D. Ross's prima facie duties (fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, self-improvement, non-maleficence); Threshold deontology (rules can be overridden at sufficient stakes); Distinction from consequentialism
primary_use_case: Normative ethical theory in academic philosophy; foundation for human-rights discourse and international law; bioethics (informed consent, truth-telling); business ethics; professional ethics; basis for arguments against utilitarian calculations that treat persons as fungible aggregators of welfare.
common_criticisms: Rule-conflict problems: when duties conflict (truth-telling vs preventing harm), strict deontology offers limited guidance; counterintuitive consequences in specific cases (the famous Murderer at the Door problem — strict Kant says don't lie, even to a murderer asking where his intended victim is hiding); abstraction from consequences seems to permit catastrophic outcomes when 'principles' are followed regardless; the Universal Law formulation has been critiqued as too permissive (almost any maxim can be universalized with enough specification) or too restrictive; cross-cultural variation in what counts as duty raises relativism concerns; tension between Kant's universalism and his historically embedded views on race and gender, which contemporary Kantianism has had to confront.
primary_sources: Kant, I. (1785). Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals; Kant, I. (1788). Critique of Practical Reason; Ross, W.D. (1930). The Right and the Good

name: Consequentialism
one_line_summary: Moral worth of action determined by its outcomes; utilitarianism is its most influential variant.
extended_summary: Consequentialism is the family of normative ethical theories holding that the moral worth of an action is determined exclusively by its consequences — by the goodness of the states of affairs it produces or could be expected to produce. The most influential variant is Utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill), which specifies the relevant good as well-being or welfare aggregated across all affected parties. Consequentialism's distinguishing claims are that no action is intrinsically right or wrong (only outcomes are), that the right action in any situation is the one that produces the best outcomes (or expected outcomes, on standard variants), and that all morally relevant considerations are reducible to outcome evaluation. Contemporary consequentialism encompasses many variants: act- vs rule-consequentialism, hedonistic vs preference vs objective-list theories of welfare, total vs average utilitarianism, agent-neutral vs agent-relative variants, and effective altruism (a contemporary movement applying consequentialist reasoning to charitable giving and career choice). Consequentialism stands in contrast to deontology on whether intrinsic act-features or outcomes are morally fundamental.
originators: Jeremy Bentham; John Stuart Mill (utilitarianism); contemporary contributors including R.M. Hare, Peter Singer, Derek Parfit
year_or_decade: Late 18th-19th century (Bentham, Mill); ongoing development through 20th-21st centuries
core_components: Outcomes as exclusively morally relevant; Maximization principle (best expected outcome); Distinction between act- and rule-consequentialism; Theory of the good (hedonistic, preference, objective-list welfare); Total vs average aggregation; Agent-neutral vs agent-relative; Connection to expected utility theory; Effective altruism as contemporary applied consequentialism; Distinction from deontology and virtue ethics
primary_use_case: Normative ethical theory; policy analysis and cost-benefit analysis; bioethics including triage and resource allocation; effective altruism movement and charitable-giving evaluation; foundation for some economic frameworks (welfare economics); applied ethics across domains.
common_criticisms: Demandingness objection: consequentialism may require enormous sacrifice for any small marginal good (Singer's drowning child argument); special obligations problem: consequentialism struggles to account for partial obligations to family, friends, and one's own projects; agent-neutrality conflicts with intuitive integrity (Williams's 'one thought too many'); aggregation problems: consequentialism may justify catastrophic acts to maximize total welfare; calculation tractability — predicting consequences across long causal chains is genuinely hard; rule-consequentialism risks collapsing into either act-consequentialism or deontology; effective altruism has drawn substantial recent critique for both technical (longtermism) and applied (FTX/SBF) reasons.
primary_sources: Bentham, J. (1789). An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation; Mill, J.S. (1861). Utilitarianism; Sidgwick, H. (1874). The Methods of Ethics; Parfit, D. (1984). Reasons and Persons

name: Utilitarianism
one_line_summary: Maximize aggregate well-being; classical (Bentham, Mill) and contemporary variants.
extended_summary: Utilitarianism is the dominant variant of consequentialism, holding that the right action is the one that produces the greatest aggregate welfare, happiness, or well-being among all affected parties. The classical formulation runs through Jeremy Bentham (An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation, 1789), who proposed a hedonistic calculus aggregating pleasures and pains, and John Stuart Mill (Utilitarianism, 1861), who substantially refined the framework by distinguishing higher and lower pleasures and addressing common objections. Henry Sidgwick's The Methods of Ethics (1874) provided the most rigorous classical statement. Contemporary utilitarianism encompasses substantial variation: act- vs rule-utilitarianism (does one apply the principle action-by-action or to rule-selection?); hedonistic vs preference vs welfare-list theories of utility; total vs average vs prioritarian aggregation (giving extra weight to the worst-off); two-level utilitarianism (Hare); and global utilitarianism (Pettit). Effective altruism is a contemporary movement applying largely utilitarian reasoning to charitable giving and career choice. Utilitarianism's intuitive force — that suffering and well-being matter, that we should produce more of the latter — has made it the workhorse moral framework for policy analysis and cost-benefit reasoning even where its specific claims are rejected.
originators: Jeremy Bentham; John Stuart Mill; Henry Sidgwick; precursors including William Godwin and the Mohist school in classical China
year_or_decade: 1789 (Bentham); 1861 (Mill); 1874 (Sidgwick); ongoing development
core_components: Greatest happiness principle; Aggregate welfare across all affected parties; Hedonistic, preference, or welfare-list theories of utility; Act- vs rule-utilitarianism; Total vs average aggregation; Mill's higher vs lower pleasures distinction; Two-level utilitarianism (intuitive everyday level, critical reflective level — Hare); Connection to expected utility theory in decision theory and economics; Effective altruism as contemporary applied utilitarianism
primary_use_case: Normative ethical theory; foundation for cost-benefit analysis and welfare economics; policy analysis particularly in healthcare resource allocation, environmental policy, and global development; foundation of effective altruism movement; bioethics; applied ethics across domains; intuitive moral reasoning in everyday choices.
common_criticisms: Same demandingness, integrity, and aggregation objections as broader consequentialism; utility-monster problem: a being who derives enormous utility from any input would have moral priority; experience-machine objection (Nozick): if utility is what matters, you should plug into a perpetual-pleasure machine — but most people wouldn't, suggesting other things matter; hedonism objection: pleasure isn't the only good; rule-utilitarianism either collapses into act-utilitarianism or becomes a form of deontology; longtermism (the consequentialist view that the far future overwhelms present concerns) has drawn substantial recent critique; effective altruism's 2022 FTX/SBF crisis raised concerns about utilitarian reasoning enabling fraud-justifying calculation; Williams's separateness-of-persons objection.
primary_sources: Bentham, J. (1789). An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation; Mill, J.S. (1861). Utilitarianism; Sidgwick, H. (1874). The Methods of Ethics; Singer, P. (1972). 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality', Philosophy and Public Affairs

name: Contractualism
one_line_summary: Scanlon's view that moral principles are those no one could reasonably reject.
extended_summary: Contractualism is the family of moral theories grounding moral norms in what could be the object of agreement among rational, reasonable parties. The two principal contemporary articulations descend from different lineages. T.M. Scanlon's What We Owe to Each Other (1998) articulates moral wrongness as 'an act is wrong if its performance under the circumstances would be disallowed by any set of principles for the general regulation of behavior that no one could reasonably reject as a basis for informed, unforced general agreement.' Scanlon's contractualism is grounded in the value of justifiability to others — moral principles must be defensible to each affected party individually, blocking aggregation in ways utilitarianism permits. John Rawls's contractualism, developed in A Theory of Justice (1971), uses the device of the original position with the veil of ignorance to derive principles of justice. Contractualism shares with deontology a focus on the right rather than the good and a non-aggregative structure, but grounds duty in interpersonal justifiability rather than pure rationality (Kant). Critics argue contractualism inherits aggregation problems in disguised form and struggles with non-human animals and future generations who cannot reasonably reject anything.
originators: T.M. Scanlon (contemporary contractualism); John Rawls (precursor through A Theory of Justice); historical antecedents in social contract theory (Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Kant)
year_or_decade: 1971 (Rawls); 1998 (Scanlon What We Owe); historical contract theory traditions
core_components: Moral principles as those no one could reasonably reject; Justifiability to each affected party as foundational; Distinction from utility aggregation; Personal vs impersonal complaints in Scanlon's framework; Connection to Rawls's original position and veil of ignorance; Non-aggregative structure (helping the many at substantial cost to one is hard to justify); Distinction from Hobbesian self-interest contractarianism
primary_use_case: Normative ethical theory; political philosophy and theory of justice; bioethics with strong concerns about aggregation (treatment rationing); applied ethics where individual justifiability matters; basis for arguments against aggregative utilitarianism in particular hard cases.
common_criticisms: 'Reasonable rejection' is contested — what counts as a reasonable basis for rejection is itself a moral question that the framework needs to answer without circularity; struggles with future generations and non-human animals (who cannot reasonably reject anything); aggregation problems return in disguised form (when many small harms could justify a large benefit, contractualism's individualism may produce counterintuitive results); Parfit's argument that contractualism, properly understood, converges with consequentialism reduces its distinctive claims; contractualism inherits some of deontology's action-guidance limitations; 'principles no one could reasonably reject' is a high bar that may not yield determinate answers in specific cases.
primary_sources: Rawls, J. (1971). A Theory of Justice; Scanlon, T.M. (1998). What We Owe to Each Other

name: Veil of Ignorance
one_line_summary: Choose principles of justice without knowing your own position in society.
extended_summary: The Veil of Ignorance is the central thought experiment in John Rawls's A Theory of Justice (1971), the most influential work in 20th-century political philosophy. Rawls asks readers to imagine an 'original position' in which rational parties choose principles to govern the basic structure of their society without knowing their own particular characteristics — class, race, gender, talents, conception of the good — that would bias them toward principles favoring their own position. Behind the veil, Rawls argues, parties would converge on two principles of justice, in lexical order: First, each person has equal claim to a fully adequate scheme of basic liberties compatible with the same scheme for all; Second, social and economic inequalities are arranged so that they are both (a) attached to positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity, and (b) to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged (the difference principle). The thought experiment operationalizes a Kantian commitment to impartiality and grounds principles of justice in what rational, mutually disinterested parties would choose under conditions of fair information. Rawls revised his framework substantially in Political Liberalism (1993), reframing it as a political rather than comprehensive moral conception. The Veil of Ignorance has been one of the most fertile philosophical devices of the past 50 years.
originators: John Rawls
year_or_decade: 1971 (A Theory of Justice); 1993 (Political Liberalism revision)
core_components: Original position thought experiment; Veil of Ignorance (parties don't know own characteristics); Two principles of justice (equal basic liberties; fair equality of opportunity + difference principle); Lexical priority of liberty principle; Maximin reasoning under uncertainty; Difference principle (inequalities only justified if they benefit least-advantaged); Reflective equilibrium as background methodology; Political Liberalism's later reframing
primary_use_case: Political philosophy and theory of justice; foundation for substantial subsequent work in distributive justice, global justice, intergenerational justice; applied to taxation, healthcare allocation, and social policy debates; teaching framework for thinking about impartiality and fairness; influence well beyond academic philosophy into political and policy discourse.
common_criticisms: Robert Nozick's libertarian critique in Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) argued Rawls's conclusions presuppose end-state distributive thinking that ignores legitimate historical entitlements; communitarian critique (Sandel, MacIntyre) argued the unencumbered self of the original position is a metaphysical fiction; feminist critique (Susan Moller Okin, others) noted that Rawls's original framing assumed the family as outside justice; G.A. Cohen argued Rawls's difference principle inadequately constrains personal incentive structures; capabilities approach (Sen, Nussbaum) argued primary goods are inadequate for cross-person welfare comparison; maximin reasoning behind the veil is contested as the right risk-attitude under genuine uncertainty; the original position structure has been argued to smuggle in conclusions through the design of the choice situation.
primary_sources: Rawls, J. (1971). A Theory of Justice; Rawls, J. (1993). Political Liberalism; Rawls, J. (2001). Justice as Fairness: A Restatement

name: Care Ethics
one_line_summary: Gilligan and Noddings' framework grounding ethics in relationships and responsiveness rather than abstract principle.
extended_summary: Care Ethics emerged in the early 1980s as a distinct ethical tradition, principally through Carol Gilligan's In a Different Voice (1982), which challenged Lawrence Kohlberg's stage theory of moral development by documenting that Gilligan's interview subjects (predominantly women) reasoned about moral dilemmas through a 'different voice' emphasizing relationships, responsibility, and contextual response rather than abstract principles. Nel Noddings's Caring: A Feminine Approach to Ethics and Moral Education (1984) substantially developed care ethics as a normative tradition, distinguishing the carer (one-caring) and the cared-for in caring relations and grounding moral life in the maintenance of caring relationships. Subsequent contributors include Virginia Held, Sara Ruddick (maternal thinking), Joan Tronto (political dimensions of care), and Eva Feder Kittay (dependency and care). Care ethics is now widely recognized as a major normative tradition alongside virtue ethics, deontology, and consequentialism, with substantial influence in feminist philosophy, applied ethics (especially nursing and medical ethics), political theory of care work, and contemporary discussions of dependency. The framework's distinctive claim is that abstract impartial principle-based ethics distorts the genuine moral phenomena of relationship and responsiveness that constitute much of moral life.
originators: Carol Gilligan (foundational empirical-philosophical articulation); Nel Noddings (normative tradition development); subsequent figures including Virginia Held, Sara Ruddick, Joan Tronto, Eva Feder Kittay
year_or_decade: 1982 (Gilligan's In a Different Voice); 1984 (Noddings's Caring)
core_components: Caring relationships as moral foundation; Carer (one-caring) and cared-for; Engrossment and motivational displacement (Noddings); Distinction from impartial principle-based ethics; Concrete other (over generalized other); Particularity and contextuality of moral situations; Maternal thinking as moral resource (Ruddick); Political dimensions of care (Tronto's caring democracy); Connection to virtue ethics (both character-focused) but distinguished by relational rather than individual focus
primary_use_case: Feminist philosophy and ethics; bioethics, particularly nursing ethics and end-of-life care; moral education; political theory of care work and dependency; environmental ethics (with care extended beyond humans); applied ethics where impartial-principle approaches feel inadequate to relational moral phenomena; counterweight to abstract principle-based ethics in clinical and educational practice.
common_criticisms: Initial Gilligan-Kohlberg debate raised concerns about essentialist gender claims — care ethics has been substantially developed beyond the gender-binary framing of its origins, but the popular conflation persists; partiality concerns: care ethics seems to permit (or require) favoring one's relations, which can conflict with impartial duties of justice; scaling problem: how do we extend care to strangers, distant others, or future generations who are not in current caring relations; Sandra Bartky and others have argued some care-ethics framings risk normalizing women's traditional caregiving labor; tension between Noddings's emphasis on completion-in-the-cared-for and care-receiver agency; political-economy critique that care ethics may obscure the structural conditions that make some bodies do most of the caring work.
primary_sources: Gilligan, C. (1982). In a Different Voice; Noddings, N. (1984). Caring: A Feminine Approach to Ethics and Moral Education; Held, V. (2006). The Ethics of Care; Kittay, E.F. (1999). Love's Labor

name: Pragmatism
one_line_summary: Peirce, James, Dewey: meaning and truth grounded in practical consequences and inquiry.
extended_summary: Pragmatism is the principal indigenous American philosophical tradition, founded by Charles Sanders Peirce in the 1870s through the Metaphysical Club in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and substantially developed by William James (Pragmatism: A New Name for Some Old Ways of Thinking, 1907), John Dewey (across many works including Democracy and Education 1916, Experience and Nature 1925), and George Herbert Mead. The tradition's defining commitments include the pragmatic maxim (Peirce: 'Consider what effects, that might conceivably have practical bearings, we conceive the object of our conception to have. Then, our conception of these effects is the whole of our conception of the object'); a fallibilist epistemology that treats inquiry as ongoing self-correction rather than approach to fixed truth; a process-oriented metaphysics in which reality is constituted through interaction; and a democratic political philosophy treating intelligence as socially distributed and inquiry as a community practice. The tradition was eclipsed by analytic philosophy in mid-20th-century academic philosophy but underwent substantial revival from the 1970s onward, principally through Richard Rorty (neopragmatism), Hilary Putnam, and Cheryl Misak. Pragmatism has had outsized influence beyond philosophy in education (Dewey), social science methodology (action research), legal theory (Holmes, Posner), and political theory.
originators: Charles Sanders Peirce (founder); William James, John Dewey, George Herbert Mead (classical period); 20th-century revival figures including Richard Rorty, Hilary Putnam, Cheryl Misak
year_or_decade: 1870s (Peirce's Metaphysical Club); 1907 (James's Pragmatism); 1979 (Rorty's Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature, neopragmatist revival)
core_components: Pragmatic maxim (meaning grounded in practical consequences); Fallibilism (knowledge as ongoing self-correction); Inquiry as community practice; Truth as what works in inquiry (with substantial variation across pragmatists); Anti-foundationalism; Process metaphysics; Connection between thought and action; Dewey's instrumentalism; Democracy as inquiry; Distinction from positivism (broader conception of what 'works')
primary_use_case: Foundational American philosophical tradition; basis for Dewey's progressive education theory; influence on legal realism (Holmes); methodological foundation for action research and design research; influence on contemporary philosophy of science and language; resource for contemporary debates about truth, objectivity, and democratic inquiry; basis for some contemporary political theories of inquiry.
common_criticisms: Critics including Bertrand Russell argued early pragmatism conflated truth with utility, with disturbing implications for what 'works' in totalitarian contexts; James's particular formulations were sometimes loose enough to invite caricature ('the cash-value of truth'); Rorty's later neopragmatism abandoned much of the classical tradition's substantive metaphysics, leading some classical pragmatists to argue Rorty wasn't really pragmatist; pragmatism's anti-foundationalism makes specific claims hard to evaluate against; tradition's diversity (classical, neo-, analytical) creates which-pragmatism-when ambiguity; some critics argue pragmatism sacrifices realism and objectivity in ways that don't survive close examination.
primary_sources: Peirce, C.S. (1878). 'How to Make Our Ideas Clear', Popular Science Monthly; James, W. (1907). Pragmatism; Dewey, J. (1925). Experience and Nature; Rorty, R. (1979). Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature

name: Existentialism
one_line_summary: Existence precedes essence; meaning is created through choice, freedom, and responsibility.
extended_summary: Existentialism is the philosophical tradition emphasizing the priority of individual existence — concrete, situated, freely choosing human existence — over abstract essence or universal nature. Soren Kierkegaard (mid-19th century) and Friedrich Nietzsche (late 19th century) are the principal precursors, with the explicitly named existentialist movement emerging in 20th-century continental philosophy through Karl Jaspers, Martin Heidegger (Being and Time 1927), Jean-Paul Sartre (Being and Nothingness 1943), Simone de Beauvoir (The Second Sex 1949), Albert Camus (The Myth of Sisyphus 1942), and Maurice Merleau-Ponty. Sartre's slogan 'existence precedes essence' captures the framework's distinctive commitment: humans first exist, encounter themselves, surge up in the world, and only then define themselves through choice, distinguishing humans from objects or natural beings whose essence (purpose, defining nature) precedes existence. Other recurring themes include radical freedom and the responsibility it produces (Sartre's 'condemned to be free'); authenticity vs bad faith (Sartre); being-toward-death and care (Heidegger); the absurd (Camus); and the inherent embodied situatedness of consciousness (Merleau-Ponty). Existentialism has had substantial influence on 20th-century literature, theology (Tillich, Bultmann, Marcel), psychotherapy (Viktor Frankl, Rollo May, Irvin Yalom), and Western culture more broadly.
originators: Kierkegaard and Nietzsche (precursors); 20th-century existentialists including Heidegger, Jaspers, Sartre, de Beauvoir, Camus, Merleau-Ponty, Marcel
year_or_decade: Mid-19th century precursors (Kierkegaard); 1927 (Heidegger Being and Time); 1943 (Sartre Being and Nothingness); 1945-60s (cultural peak)
core_components: Existence precedes essence (Sartre); Radical freedom and responsibility; Authenticity vs bad faith; Being-toward-death (Heidegger); The absurd (Camus); Anxiety/angst as encounter with freedom; Embodied situated consciousness (Merleau-Ponty); Beauvoir's situated ethics and feminist existentialism; Theistic vs atheistic variants (Kierkegaard, Marcel vs Sartre, Camus)
primary_use_case: 20th-century continental philosophy, with continuing influence; existential psychotherapy (Frankl's logotherapy, Yalom's existential psychotherapy); theology (Tillich, Bultmann); literature (Sartre, Camus, Beckett, Kafka adjacent); cultural framing for individual freedom and authenticity; foundation for some contemporary phenomenology and embodied-cognition work.
common_criticisms: Diverse tradition that resists single definition — Heidegger explicitly rejected 'existentialist' label; Sartre's emphasis on radical individual freedom underweights social, structural, and embodied constraints (de Beauvoir addressed some of this within the tradition); 'authenticity' framing can rationalize self-indulgence and ignore obligation; popular existentialism (1960s cultural moment) often reduced complex philosophical positions to slogans; Heidegger's Nazi engagement raised lasting questions about the ethical implications of his philosophy; Sartre's later Marxism complicated his earlier individualist framing; the tradition's focus on dramatic confrontation with anxiety and freedom may be culturally specific to mid-20th-century European bourgeois experience.
primary_sources: Kierkegaard, S. (1843, 1844, 1849). Various works; Nietzsche, F. (1883-1888). Various works; Heidegger, M. (1927). Being and Time; Sartre, J.-P. (1943). Being and Nothingness; de Beauvoir, S. (1949). The Second Sex; Camus, A. (1942). The Myth of Sisyphus

name: Phenomenology
one_line_summary: Husserl's method of describing structures of conscious experience as they appear.
extended_summary: Phenomenology is the philosophical method and tradition founded by Edmund Husserl in the early 20th century, focused on describing the structures of conscious experience as they are given to consciousness, prior to and apart from any theoretical reduction or scientific abstraction. Husserl's foundational works (Logical Investigations 1900-1901, Ideas Pertaining to a Pure Phenomenology 1913) developed the phenomenological method through the epoche (suspension of the natural attitude's assumptions about external reality) and phenomenological reduction (attending to phenomena as they appear in pure consciousness). Key concepts include intentionality (consciousness is always consciousness of something), the noema-noesis structure (the act of consciousness and its intentional content), and the lifeworld (the pre-theoretical world of meaning we live in). Subsequent figures developed the tradition substantially: Heidegger turned phenomenology toward the analysis of human existence (Dasein) in Being and Time (1927); Merleau-Ponty articulated embodied phenomenology in Phenomenology of Perception (1945); Sartre integrated phenomenology with existentialism; Levinas turned phenomenology toward the ethical encounter with the other; and contemporary figures including Dan Zahavi, Shaun Gallagher, and Evan Thompson have integrated phenomenology with cognitive science. The tradition is foundational to continental philosophy and increasingly influential in cognitive science, particularly in 4E (embodied, embedded, enactive, extended) cognition research.
originators: Edmund Husserl (founder); subsequent figures including Martin Heidegger, Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Jean-Paul Sartre, Emmanuel Levinas, Edith Stein
year_or_decade: 1900-1901 (Husserl's Logical Investigations); 1913 (Ideas); ongoing tradition through 20th-21st centuries
core_components: Phenomenological method: epoche (suspension of natural attitude) and reduction; Intentionality (consciousness is consciousness of something); Noema (intentional object) and noesis (intentional act); Lifeworld (pre-theoretical world of meaning); Embodiment (Merleau-Ponty); Hermeneutic phenomenology (Heidegger, Gadamer); Phenomenological psychology and psychiatry (Jaspers, Binswanger); Connection to 4E cognition research; Distinction from naturalistic empirical psychology
primary_use_case: Continental philosophy and philosophy of mind; foundation for hermeneutics, existentialism, and post-structuralism; methodological resource in qualitative research (phenomenological psychology, nursing research); growing integration with cognitive science and 4E cognition research; foundation for some approaches to consciousness studies; influence on phenomenologically-oriented psychiatry and psychotherapy.
common_criticisms: Method's reliance on first-person introspective reports raises substantial methodological concerns about reliability, theory-ladenness, and verification; the epoche's suspension of natural-attitude assumptions is contested as either impossible or unhelpful; tradition's diversity (Husserlian transcendental, Heideggerian existential, Merleau-Ponty's embodied, Levinas's ethical) creates which-phenomenology-when ambiguity; Husserl's transcendental idealism in later work has been argued to undermine the original descriptive program; integration with cognitive science is genuinely productive in some areas but raises tensions between phenomenology's anti-naturalistic origins and naturalistic methods; tradition is dense and stylistically demanding, limiting accessibility.
primary_sources: Husserl, E. (1900-1901). Logical Investigations; Husserl, E. (1913). Ideas Pertaining to a Pure Phenomenology; Heidegger, M. (1927). Being and Time; Merleau-Ponty, M. (1945). Phenomenology of Perception

name: Hermeneutics
one_line_summary: Theory and practice of interpretation, especially of texts and historical understanding.
extended_summary: Hermeneutics is the theory and practice of interpretation, with roots in biblical and legal exegesis traditions extending back to antiquity. Modern philosophical hermeneutics emerged through Friedrich Schleiermacher's general hermeneutics in the early 19th century (extending interpretive methods beyond sacred texts to all language), Wilhelm Dilthey's distinction between explanation (in natural sciences) and understanding (Verstehen, in human sciences), Martin Heidegger's ontological turn that made interpretation a fundamental mode of being-in-the-world (Being and Time, 1927), and most influentially Hans-Georg Gadamer's Truth and Method (1960), which articulated hermeneutic experience as fundamental to human understanding generally. Key concepts include the hermeneutic circle (understanding part requires understanding whole and vice versa); fusion of horizons (interpretation as encounter between interpreter's horizon and text's horizon); effective historical consciousness (recognition that interpretation occurs within tradition); and the productive role of prejudice (Vorurteil, prior understanding) in interpretation. Paul Ricoeur's hermeneutics of suspicion vs hermeneutics of trust (engaging Marx, Nietzsche, Freud) and Jurgen Habermas's critique of Gadamer (insisting on critical reflection on tradition) extend the tradition. Hermeneutics is foundational to continental philosophy and has substantial influence in literary theory, theology, legal interpretation, and qualitative research methodology.
originators: Friedrich Schleiermacher (general hermeneutics); Wilhelm Dilthey (Verstehen); Martin Heidegger (ontological turn); Hans-Georg Gadamer (philosophical hermeneutics); Paul Ricoeur, Jurgen Habermas, Emilio Betti
year_or_decade: Schleiermacher early 19th century; Dilthey late 19th century; Heidegger 1927; Gadamer 1960 (Truth and Method)
core_components: Hermeneutic circle (whole and parts); Fusion of horizons (Gadamer); Effective historical consciousness; Productive role of prejudice/prior understanding; Distinction between explanation (natural science) and understanding (human science); Hermeneutic of suspicion vs hermeneutic of trust (Ricoeur); Phronesis as hermeneutic virtue; Habermas's emphasis on critical reflection on tradition; Application to texts, history, art, social practices, and self-understanding
primary_use_case: Continental philosophy and philosophy of human sciences; literary theory and criticism; theology and biblical interpretation; legal interpretation theory; qualitative research methodology in social sciences; foundation for some approaches to historical understanding; influence on philosophical anthropology and cultural theory.
common_criticisms: Habermas-Gadamer debate raised substantive concerns about hermeneutics' conservatism — Gadamer's emphasis on tradition can underweight the role of critical reflection in escaping ideological distortion; relativism concerns: if all interpretation is horizon-bound, can we adjudicate between competing interpretations?; hermeneutic-circle structure has been argued to risk circular reasoning when applied without methodological discipline; integration with empirical methods is genuinely difficult; tradition's denseness limits accessibility; competing schools (Schleiermacher's romantic hermeneutics, Dilthey's psychological, Gadamer's ontological, Ricoeur's, Betti's objectivist) create which-hermeneutics-when ambiguity; Anglo-American analytic philosophy has largely been skeptical of the tradition.
primary_sources: Schleiermacher, F. (1819 lectures, posthumous). Hermeneutics; Dilthey, W. (1900). 'The Rise of Hermeneutics'; Gadamer, H.-G. (1960). Truth and Method; Ricoeur, P. (1981). Hermeneutics and the Human Sciences

name: Stoicism
one_line_summary: Hellenistic philosophy emphasizing virtue, reason, and acceptance of what one cannot control.
extended_summary: Stoicism was founded by Zeno of Citium in Athens around 300 BCE, named for the Stoa Poikile (Painted Porch) where he taught, and developed through three principal periods: the Early Stoa (Zeno, Cleanthes, Chrysippus — 3rd century BCE, foundational logic, physics, and ethics); the Middle Stoa (Panaetius, Posidonius — 2nd-1st century BCE, modified the system for Roman audiences); and the Late or Roman Stoa (Seneca, Musonius Rufus, Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius — 1st-2nd century CE, with surviving works concentrated in this period). The Stoic system integrates logic (including foundational propositional logic), physics (a corporealist, deterministic, providential cosmos), and ethics (the only good is virtue; emotions are mistaken value-judgments to be transformed; one should live according to nature/reason). The dichotomy of control — distinguishing what is up to us (our judgments, intentions, desires, aversions) from what is not (external events, others' actions, our reputation, our bodies in many respects) and focusing on the former — is the most operationally famous element. Stoicism has had two major revivals: the Renaissance/early modern (Lipsius's neostoicism, influence on Spinoza); and the contemporary practical-philosophy revival (Pierre Hadot's reframing of ancient philosophy as spiritual exercise, popular books by William Irvine, Massimo Pigliucci, Ryan Holiday, the Modern Stoicism movement). The contemporary revival has substantial overlap with cognitive-behavioral therapy — Albert Ellis explicitly cited Stoic influence on REBT, and CBT's identification of distorted appraisals as the source of distress closely tracks the Stoic analysis of passions.
originators: Zeno of Citium (founder); Chrysippus (substantial systematic development); Late Stoa figures Seneca, Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius (most accessible surviving works)
year_or_decade: ~300 BCE (Zeno); 1st-2nd century CE (Roman Stoa surviving texts); 21st century (contemporary practical revival)
core_components: Three pillars: Logic, Physics, Ethics; Virtue as the only good (everything else is preferred indifferent or dispreferred indifferent); Dichotomy of control (Epictetus's Discourses); Apatheia (freedom from disturbing passions, not absence of feeling); Cosmopolitanism (citizen of the world); Living according to nature/reason; Premeditatio malorum (negative visualization); Spiritual exercises; Connection to CBT (Ellis explicitly cited Stoic influence on REBT)
primary_use_case: Foundational Hellenistic philosophical school; major historical influence on Western ethical and political thought; contemporary practical-philosophy revival with substantial popular following; integration with CBT and other modern psychotherapies; foundation for resilience training in military and high-stress professional contexts; influence on contemporary virtue ethics and philosophy of emotion.
common_criticisms: Apatheia (freedom from disturbing passions) can be misread as emotional suppression rather than the Stoic-intended cognitive transformation of value judgments; the dichotomy of control is contested when applied to clearly partial control (we have substantial influence over many things that aren't fully 'up to us'); contemporary popularization (especially Ryan Holiday and similar) sometimes flattens the framework into self-help slogans, missing the underlying philosophical system; the Stoic claim that virtue is sufficient for happiness is counterintuitive and difficult to defend in cases of severe suffering; cosmopolitan elements coexist with Stoic acceptance of social hierarchy in ways modern adopters often elide; Christian appropriations of Stoic concepts changed their meaning substantively; Stoic determinism creates tensions with the framework's strong commitment to moral responsibility.
primary_sources: Epictetus. Discourses and Enchiridion (compiled by Arrian, c. 108 CE); Seneca. Letters from a Stoic (1st century CE); Marcus Aurelius. Meditations (c. 170-180 CE); Hadot, P. (1995). Philosophy as a Way of Life
siblings: Epicureanism; Virtue Ethics; Stoic Dichotomy of Control

name: Epicureanism
one_line_summary: Hellenistic philosophy seeking tranquility through prudent pleasure and absence of pain.
extended_summary: Epicureanism was founded by Epicurus (341-270 BCE) in his Athenian school, the Garden, and substantially preserved through the Roman poet Lucretius's De Rerum Natura (On the Nature of Things, 1st century BCE) and the surviving fragments of Epicurus's writings. The system integrates atomistic physics (drawn from Democritus, modified by Epicurus's swerve to allow for free will), an empiricist epistemology (sensations and prolepses as criteria of truth), and a hedonist ethics with substantial nuance: pleasure is indeed the goal of life, but the highest pleasure is ataraxia (tranquility, freedom from anxiety) and aponia (absence of bodily pain), achieved not through maximal sensory indulgence but through prudent moderation, friendship, philosophical understanding, and the elimination of unfounded fears (especially fear of death and fear of the gods). Epicurus's tetrapharmakos (fourfold remedy) summarizes: God is not to be feared; death is nothing to us (we are not present to experience our nonexistence); good is easy to attain; evil is easy to endure. Epicureanism declined after the rise of Christianity (its materialism and rejection of providential gods made it unpalatable) and was rediscovered through Lucretius in the Renaissance, with substantial influence on early modern atomism, materialism, and Enlightenment thought.
originators: Epicurus (founder); Metrodorus, Hermarchus (early followers); Lucretius (Roman expositor and preserver)
year_or_decade: ~307 BCE (Epicurus founds the Garden); 1st century BCE (Lucretius); Renaissance rediscovery via Lucretius
core_components: Atomism (atoms and void as fundamental); The swerve (clinamen, allowing free will); Empiricist epistemology (sensations and prolepses); Pleasure as ethical goal, but ataraxia (tranquility) as highest pleasure; Aponia (absence of pain); Tetrapharmakos (fourfold remedy); Distinction between necessary, natural-but-not-necessary, and vain desires; Death is nothing to us (no experiencer); Friendship as central good; Withdrawal from political life ('live unnoticed')
primary_use_case: Foundational Hellenistic philosophical school; major historical influence on materialist and naturalist traditions; influence on Lucretian atomism, early modern philosophy (Hobbes, Gassendi), and Enlightenment thought (Diderot, Jefferson); contemporary practical-philosophy interest alongside Stoicism revival; foundation for some contemporary discussions of well-being and minimalism.
common_criticisms: Caricatured throughout history as crude hedonism (the modern colloquial 'epicurean' inverts the original meaning) — Epicurus actually advocated simple pleasures and warned against indulgence; popular reception has consistently failed to engage the framework's atomistic-epistemological substructure; argument that 'death is nothing to us' (since we're not present to experience our death) is contested by responses including the deprivation account (death deprives us of future goods); withdrawal from political life ('live unnoticed') sits awkwardly with civic obligations; tetrapharmakos's optimistic 'evil is easy to endure' is hard to maintain in cases of severe suffering; Christian opposition produced enduring negative reception in much of Western tradition; less prominent contemporary revival than Stoicism despite arguably similar therapeutic potential.
primary_sources: Epicurus. Letters to Herodotus, Pythocles, and Menoeceus; Principal Doctrines; Vatican Sayings (surviving fragments); Lucretius. De Rerum Natura (On the Nature of Things); Greenblatt, S. (2011). The Swerve: How the World Became Modern (cultural history)

name: Falsificationism
one_line_summary: Popper's criterion that scientific claims must be capable of being proven wrong.
extended_summary: Falsificationism was developed by Karl Popper, presented in The Logic of Scientific Discovery (originally Logik der Forschung, 1934; English translation 1959) and elaborated in subsequent works including Conjectures and Refutations (1963). Popper proposed falsifiability as the criterion of demarcation between scientific and non-scientific claims: a theory is scientific if and only if it is capable of being refuted by some possible observation, regardless of whether the refutation has actually occurred. The motivating insight was Popper's observation that Marxism and Freudian psychoanalysis seemed to explain everything that happened — there was no observation their adherents would accept as refuting the theory — while Einstein's general relativity made specific risky predictions that could have been refuted (and indeed could have been disconfirmed in the 1919 eclipse observations). For Popper, science proceeds not by induction from observations but through bold conjectures that survive attempts at refutation, with knowledge growing through elimination of false theories. Subsequent philosophy of science complicated this picture substantially: Quine-Duhem holism (we test webs of beliefs, not isolated propositions, so falsifications don't unambiguously target specific claims); Kuhn's paradigm shifts (science doesn't proceed through accumulated falsifications but through revolutionary changes); Lakatos's research programmes (theories have hard cores protected by auxiliary hypothesis adjustments); Feyerabend's anarchism. Falsificationism remains influential in scientific self-understanding (especially in physics and parts of biology) but is no longer the dominant philosophy-of-science position.
originators: Karl Popper
year_or_decade: 1934 (Logik der Forschung); 1959 (English translation); 1963 (Conjectures and Refutations)
core_components: Falsifiability as demarcation criterion (scientific vs non-scientific); Asymmetry of confirmation and falsification; Bold conjectures as scientific virtue; Risky predictions; Critique of induction; Science as conjecture-and-refutation; Critical rationalism (broader Popperian methodology); Distinction between strict refutability and degrees of falsifiability; Connection to open society and political philosophy
primary_use_case: Philosophy of science and scientific methodology; demarcation between science and non-science (notably in critiques of pseudoscience); scientific self-understanding particularly in physics; influence on Imre Lakatos's research programmes; pedagogical framework in philosophy of science education; basis for arguments that some prominent scientific claims are insufficiently testable.
common_criticisms: Quine-Duhem holism: we test theories together with auxiliary hypotheses, so any failed prediction can be saved by adjusting auxiliary assumptions rather than rejecting the target hypothesis; Kuhn's argument that science doesn't actually proceed by falsification — paradigms persist despite anomalies until alternatives mature; Lakatos's argument that even Einstein's GR was treated by physicists as 'protected' by auxiliary adjustments rather than refuted; Bayesian critiques argue probabilistic confirmation, not deductive refutation, is the actual structure of scientific reasoning; falsifiability is a graduated rather than binary property — many genuinely scientific claims are difficult to test; Popper's account doesn't well capture historical sciences (cosmology, evolutionary biology, paleontology) where some claims are about unrepeatable past events; falsificationism in popular use sometimes becomes 'pseudoscience accusation' deployed without engaging actual evidence.
primary_sources: Popper, K. (1934/1959). The Logic of Scientific Discovery; Popper, K. (1963). Conjectures and Refutations; Popper, K. (1972). Objective Knowledge
siblings: Paradigm Shift; Lakatosian Research Programmes; Bayesian Epistemology

name: Paradigm Shift
one_line_summary: Kuhn's account of science as alternating periods of normal science and revolutionary change.
extended_summary: Thomas Kuhn's The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) argued against the gradual accumulationist picture of scientific progress, presenting science as alternating between periods of 'normal science' (puzzle-solving within an established paradigm — a comprehensive framework of theory, methods, examples, and standards shared by a scientific community) and periods of crisis and revolutionary change in which an accumulating set of anomalies that cannot be resolved within the prevailing paradigm leads to a fundamental restructuring of the field's framework. The shift from Ptolemaic to Copernican astronomy, from phlogiston to oxygen chemistry, from Newtonian to Einsteinian physics, and from classical to quantum mechanics are Kuhn's canonical examples. Critically, Kuhn argued that competing paradigms are 'incommensurable' — they may use the same words ('mass', 'space', 'planet') with substantively different meanings, and there is no neutral observation language by which to compare them. The Postscript to the second edition (1969) and Kuhn's later work substantially refined and clarified his concepts in response to critiques. The book substantially shaped subsequent philosophy of science (Lakatos, Feyerabend, Laudan responded directly), reshaped historiography of science, and gave the wider culture the term 'paradigm shift' for any fundamental conceptual change — usually applied much more loosely than Kuhn intended.
originators: Thomas S. Kuhn
year_or_decade: 1962 (The Structure of Scientific Revolutions); 1969 (Postscript with revisions in 2nd edition)
core_components: Normal science (puzzle-solving within paradigm); Paradigm (theory + methods + examples + standards + community); Anomalies (puzzles that resist solution); Crisis and revolutionary change; Paradigm shift (revolutionary change in framework); Incommensurability (competing paradigms have no neutral observation language); Exemplars (concrete problem-solutions that train scientists); Distinction from Popperian falsificationism (paradigms aren't simply abandoned on first refuting evidence); Pre-paradigm (immature science before unification)
primary_use_case: Philosophy of science and history of science; foundation for substantial subsequent work in sociology of scientific knowledge (Bloor, Latour); reframing of how scientific change actually occurs; teaching framework in philosophy of science; widely (and often loosely) applied vocabulary in business and culture for fundamental conceptual change; basis for arguments about discipline-bound limits of inquiry.
common_criticisms: Strong incommensurability claim has been substantially contested — successful translation between paradigms is possible in many cases, and Kuhn himself softened the claim in later work; charge of relativism: if paradigm changes are not driven by accumulating evidence, in what sense is science progressive? (Kuhn's answers were not universally satisfying); 'paradigm' is used in many incompatible senses across the book — Margaret Masterman's 1970 paper identified 21 uses; popular adoption has substantially diluted the concept, with 'paradigm shift' applied to any moderate change; Kuhn's account works better for some sciences (physics, chemistry at scale) than others (biology, where multiple paradigms often coexist); the model is empirically grounded in selected historical cases that some historians of science have argued were retrospectively shaped to fit; tension between Kuhn's descriptive account and any normative philosophy of science.
primary_sources: Kuhn, T.S. (1962, 2nd ed. 1969 with Postscript, 50th anniversary ed. 2012). The Structure of Scientific Revolutions; Kuhn, T.S. (1977). The Essential Tension

name: Lakatosian Research Programmes
one_line_summary: Lakatos' refinement of Popper: programmes have hard cores and protective belts of auxiliary hypotheses.
extended_summary: Imre Lakatos's Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes, presented in his 1970 paper 'Falsification and the Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes' (in Lakatos and Musgrave's Criticism and the Growth of Knowledge), articulates a synthesis between Popper's falsificationism and Kuhn's account of paradigms. Lakatos argued that scientific theories should be evaluated not as isolated falsifiable propositions but as research programmes — extended structures comprising a 'hard core' of central commitments treated as irrefutable by methodological decision, surrounded by a 'protective belt' of auxiliary hypotheses that absorb adjustments in light of anomalies. A research programme is 'progressive' when its successive theory adjustments predict novel facts that are subsequently corroborated, and 'degenerating' when adjustments are merely ad hoc accommodations of anomalies without novel predictive success. Programmes should be abandoned not at first failed prediction (Popper's stricter view) nor only through revolutionary replacement (Kuhn's view) but when they degenerate while a competing progressive programme is available. Lakatos's account preserves Popper's commitment to the rationality of science while accommodating the Kuhnian observation that scientists don't simply abandon theories on first refuting evidence. The framework has been substantial in philosophy of science and economics methodology (where Lakatos's work was specifically influential).
originators: Imre Lakatos
year_or_decade: 1970 (foundational paper); 1978 (The Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes posthumous)
core_components: Research programme as unit of evaluation (not isolated theory); Hard core (central commitments treated as irrefutable by methodological decision); Protective belt (auxiliary hypotheses adjusted to accommodate anomalies); Progressive vs degenerating problemshifts; Novel predictions corroborated as marker of progress; Competing programmes as basis for choice; Synthesis of Popperian falsificationism and Kuhnian paradigms; Distinction between sophisticated and naive falsificationism
primary_use_case: Philosophy of science as bridge between Popper and Kuhn; methodology in economics (where Lakatos was directly influential through Mark Blaug and others); evaluation of long-running scientific debates and theory programmes; teaching framework in philosophy of science; resource for distinguishing legitimate theory adjustments from ad hoc rescue.
common_criticisms: Distinction between 'novel' predictions and 'ad hoc' adjustments is itself contested — what counts as novel can be argued retrospectively; 'progressive' vs 'degenerating' classifications often only become clear in hindsight, limiting the framework's prescriptive force; the methodology preserves the rationality of science partly by retreating to hindsight evaluation, weakening its real-time guidance; the hard core's irrefutability is by methodological decision rather than logical necessity, which raises questions about how the decision is justified; Lakatos's account doesn't well capture revolutions in pre-paradigm sciences or sciences with multiple coexisting programmes; integration with Bayesian and statistical accounts of evidence has been limited; less popular than Kuhn or Popper in contemporary philosophy of science.
primary_sources: Lakatos, I. (1970). 'Falsification and the Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes', in Lakatos & Musgrave (eds.) Criticism and the Growth of Knowledge; Lakatos, I. (1978). The Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes

name: Bayesian Epistemology
band_notes: Distinct from Bayesian Inference (formal-scientific); this is the philosophical position that belief should be modeled probabilistically.
one_line_summary: Belief modeled as probability and updated by Bayes' rule on new evidence.
extended_summary: Bayesian Epistemology is the philosophical position that rational degrees of belief (credences) should be modeled as probabilities satisfying the axioms of probability theory, and that rational belief revision in light of new evidence should follow Bayes's theorem (updating prior probabilities to posterior probabilities by conditioning on new evidence). The framework draws on Frank Ramsey's 1926 'Truth and Probability' and Bruno de Finetti's 1937 'La prevision' for foundational Dutch Book arguments showing that an agent whose credences violate probability axioms can be exploited through bets. Subsequent contributors include Rudolf Carnap (logical probability), Richard Jeffrey (probability kinematics for uncertain evidence), Patrick Maher, and contemporary figures including Branden Fitelson, James Joyce, and Kevin Kelly. Bayesian epistemology offers a unified account of confirmation, evidential support, learning, and inference, with applications to philosophy of science (Bayesian confirmation theory), formal epistemology, decision theory under uncertainty, and the philosophy of induction. The framework is distinct from Bayesian Inference as practiced in statistics and machine learning (where it is formal-scientific) — the philosophical position is that belief itself should be probabilistically modeled, not just that probabilistic methods are useful tools. The framework has substantial subjective and objective variants, with the subjective Bayesian permitting wide latitude in priors and the objective Bayesian seeking principled constraints on prior selection.
originators: Frank P. Ramsey (foundational Dutch Book argument); Bruno de Finetti (subjective probability foundations); Rudolf Carnap (logical probability); contemporary figures including Richard Jeffrey, Patrick Maher, James Joyce, Branden Fitelson
year_or_decade: 1926 (Ramsey); 1937 (de Finetti); 1962 (Carnap Logical Foundations of Probability); ongoing development
core_components: Credences (degrees of belief) modeled as probabilities; Probability axioms (non-negativity, normalization, additivity); Bayes' theorem for belief updating; Dutch Book argument (probabilistic incoherence enables exploitation); Conditionalization as rational update rule; Jeffrey conditionalization for uncertain evidence; Subjective vs objective Bayesianism; Connection to decision theory under uncertainty; Distinction from frequentist statistics
primary_use_case: Formal epistemology and philosophy of science; philosophical foundations for statistical methodology; theory of confirmation and evidence; decision theory under uncertainty; foundation for some contemporary discussions of rationality; growing influence in cognitive science and computational rationality research; influence on rationalist communities (LessWrong, effective altruism) for everyday reasoning.
common_criticisms: Problem of priors: in subjective Bayesianism, priors can be arbitrary, and yet evidence interpretation depends on them; objective Bayesianism's attempts to constrain priors (maximum entropy, indifference principles) have not produced consensus; old evidence problem: Bayesian conditionalization works poorly for evidence already known to the agent; logical omniscience problem: standard Bayesianism assumes agents have perfect logical and mathematical knowledge, which no real agent does; 'lottery paradox' and similar puzzles for the relationship between credences and binary belief; integration with empirical research on actual human reasoning is mixed — humans systematically deviate from Bayesian updating in characterizable ways; the framework's mathematical sophistication can obscure substantive philosophical commitments; competing frameworks including Dempster-Shafer theory and imprecise probabilities argue Bayesianism is too restrictive.
primary_sources: Ramsey, F.P. (1926). 'Truth and Probability'; de Finetti, B. (1937). 'La prevision: ses lois logiques, ses sources subjectives'; Joyce, J.M. (1998). 'A Nonpragmatic Vindication of Probabilism'; Bovens, L. & Hartmann, S. (2003). Bayesian Epistemology

name: Reflective Equilibrium
one_line_summary: Iterative adjustment between principles and considered judgments until coherence is reached.
extended_summary: Reflective Equilibrium is the methodological framework articulated by John Rawls in A Theory of Justice (1971) for justifying moral and political principles through iterative adjustment between general principles and considered particular judgments until they reach mutual coherence. The method's structure: begin with considered judgments (particular moral intuitions held with relative certainty under conditions favoring careful reflection — not snap reactions or socially-pressured views); articulate candidate principles that account for those judgments; identify cases where principles conflict with considered judgments; revise either principles or judgments (whichever is more reasonable to revise in the specific case) and iterate. 'Wide' reflective equilibrium, distinguished from narrow, additionally considers competing background theories (philosophical, social-scientific) that inform both principles and judgments, with all three levels mutually adjusting. The framework descends from Nelson Goodman's Fact, Fiction, and Forecast (1955) account of justifying inductive principles and is closely related to coherentist epistemology more generally. Reflective equilibrium is now the dominant methodological framework in normative ethics, political philosophy, and applied ethics, even where its specific commitments are contested. Critics argue it provides too much latitude (almost any principle can be made to fit suitably-revised judgments), defends starting points (considered judgments) that may themselves be culturally biased, or risks circular reasoning.
originators: John Rawls (in moral and political philosophy); Nelson Goodman (foundational antecedent in epistemology); Norman Daniels (development of wide reflective equilibrium)
year_or_decade: 1955 (Goodman antecedent); 1971 (Rawls A Theory of Justice); 1979 (Daniels 'Wide Reflective Equilibrium and Theory Acceptance in Ethics')
core_components: Considered judgments (particular intuitions held under careful reflection); General principles (candidate accounts of those judgments); Iterative mutual adjustment; Narrow vs wide reflective equilibrium (wide includes background theories); Distinction from foundationalism (no privileged starting point); Connection to coherentism in epistemology; Application across normative ethics, political philosophy, and applied ethics; Distinction between considered judgments and mere intuitions or socially-shaped reactions
primary_use_case: Methodology in normative ethics, political philosophy, and applied ethics; foundation for Rawls's derivation of his principles of justice; widely-used framework in bioethics, business ethics, and other applied fields; basis for arguments about how to balance theoretical principles against case-specific intuitions; pedagogical framework for ethics teaching.
common_criticisms: Considered judgments may themselves be culturally biased — the method's bootstrap problem is that we can only start from where we are, and where we are may be substantially mistaken; circular reasoning concern: principles are tested against judgments that we've already adjusted to fit principles; unclear when iteration should stop — equilibrium is rarely complete and final; doesn't adequately distinguish good revisions of judgments (in light of better principles) from bad revisions (rationalizing comfortable principles); wide reflective equilibrium adds more degrees of freedom but also more potential for justification through preferred-theory selection; can become a cover for confirming pre-existing views by selectively adjusting judgments; some critics argue the method is a dressed-up appeal to intuition with extra steps.
primary_sources: Goodman, N. (1955). Fact, Fiction, and Forecast; Rawls, J. (1971). A Theory of Justice; Daniels, N. (1979). 'Wide Reflective Equilibrium and Theory Acceptance in Ethics', Journal of Philosophy

name: Foundationalism
one_line_summary: Knowledge structure resting on basic non-inferentially justified beliefs.
extended_summary: Foundationalism is the epistemological position that the structure of justified belief and knowledge is hierarchical, with non-inferentially justified 'basic' beliefs at the foundation supporting derivatively justified beliefs through inferential relations. The motivating problem is the regress of justification: if every belief requires another belief to justify it, the chain either continues forever (problematic), circles (also problematic), or terminates in beliefs that don't require further justification — foundationalism takes the third option. The tradition includes classical foundationalism (Descartes, Locke, classical empiricists, classical rationalists) holding that basic beliefs are infallibly self-evident or immediately given in experience; modest foundationalism (contemporary articulations including BonJour, Audi, Plantinga's reformed epistemology) accepting fallible non-inferential justification; and Reformed Epistemology (Plantinga, Wolterstorff) extending foundationalism to religious belief by arguing belief in God can be 'properly basic.' Foundationalism stands in opposition to coherentism (which denies the asymmetric structure between basic and derivative beliefs) and is in tension with reflective equilibrium and pragmatism. The position has been substantially under siege since the mid-20th century — Sellars's critique of the 'myth of the given', Quine's holistic critique of analyticity, and substantial coherentist alternatives have all challenged classical foundationalism — but more modest variants remain prominent in contemporary epistemology.
originators: Descartes, Locke, classical rationalist and empiricist tradition; Bertrand Russell (modern logical-empiricist variant); contemporary contributors including Roderick Chisholm, William Alston, Robert Audi, Alvin Plantinga (reformed epistemology)
year_or_decade: Classical foundationalism 17th century onward; modest contemporary variants 20th-21st century; Plantinga's reformed epistemology 1980s
core_components: Basic beliefs (non-inferentially justified); Derivative beliefs (inferentially justified by basic beliefs); Asymmetric justification structure; Solution to regress problem; Classical foundationalism (infallibility of basic beliefs); Modest foundationalism (fallible non-inferential justification); Reformed epistemology (Plantinga's properly basic religious belief); Distinction from coherentism (denies asymmetric structure); Internalism vs externalism cuts across foundationalism
primary_use_case: Foundational epistemological position in analytic philosophy; framework for thinking about epistemic justification structure; foundation for many specific epistemologies (perceptual, mathematical, religious); reference framework in philosophy of religion (Plantinga); teaching tool in epistemology education; basis for arguments about which beliefs deserve foundational status.
common_criticisms: Sellars's 'myth of the given' (1956): the supposed non-inferentially justified perceptual beliefs are not pure given but already conceptually structured, undermining classical foundationalism; Quine-Duhem holism: beliefs are tested in webs, not individually, undermining the basic/derivative distinction; difficulty specifying what makes a belief properly basic without arbitrariness; classical foundationalism's infallibility requirements are not met by any actual human beliefs; Plantinga's expansion of properly basic to include religious beliefs has been argued to make the framework permit too much; coherentist and pragmatist alternatives offer different structures that some argue better account for actual epistemic practice; tension with reliabilism and externalist alternatives; modest foundationalism may concede so much to non-foundational considerations that it loses distinct content.
primary_sources: Descartes, R. (1641). Meditations on First Philosophy; Russell, B. (1912). The Problems of Philosophy; Sellars, W. (1956). 'Empiricism and the Philosophy of Mind' (critique); BonJour, L. & Sosa, E. (2003). Epistemic Justification: Internalism vs. Externalism, Foundations vs. Virtues

name: Coherentism
one_line_summary: Knowledge justified by mutual support among beliefs, with no privileged foundation.
extended_summary: Coherentism is the epistemological position that the structure of justified belief is holistic rather than hierarchical: a belief is justified by its coherence with other beliefs in a comprehensive system, rather than by support from privileged 'basic' beliefs (as foundationalism holds). The position descends from German idealism (Hegel, Bradley, Bosanquet) but is substantially developed in the analytic tradition through W.V.O. Quine's 1951 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism' (with the metaphor of the web of belief, in which empirical findings affect any part of the web with adjustments propagating throughout), Wilfrid Sellars's critique of the myth of the given, and contemporary articulations by Laurence BonJour (The Structure of Empirical Knowledge, 1985), Keith Lehrer, and others. Coherence has been variously specified — logical consistency is the minimum, with stronger requirements including mutual entailment, explanatory unity, probabilistic coherence, and absence of countervailing relations. Coherentism's central challenge is the isolation objection: a coherent belief system might still be entirely disconnected from reality, with no input from the world. BonJour and others addressed this through observational requirements, but BonJour himself later abandoned coherentism for foundationalism over this concern. Reflective equilibrium is the most influential contemporary methodology grounded in coherentist principles.
originators: Hegelian idealist tradition; W.V.O. Quine (analytic articulation); Wilfrid Sellars (myth of the given critique); Laurence BonJour (foundational coherentist articulation, later abandoned); Keith Lehrer; Donald Davidson (related views)
year_or_decade: Idealist tradition 19th century; Quine 1951; BonJour 1985 (and 1999 abandonment)
core_components: Coherence among beliefs as justification; No privileged foundation or basic beliefs; Web of belief metaphor (Quine); Holistic confirmation; Logical consistency as minimum coherence; Stronger coherence: mutual support, explanatory unity, probabilistic coherence; Isolation objection (coherent system might be disconnected from reality); BonJour's observational requirement; Distinction from foundationalism on structure question; Connection to reflective equilibrium
primary_use_case: Foundational epistemological position in analytic philosophy; framework for thinking about justification structure; foundation for reflective equilibrium methodology in ethics; influence on philosophy of science (especially Quinean naturalized epistemology); resource for thinking about scientific theory evaluation; pedagogical framework in epistemology education.
common_criticisms: Isolation objection: a coherent belief system might still be entirely disconnected from reality, with no input from the world — BonJour himself abandoned coherentism over this concern; multiple incompatible coherent systems could each be perfectly internally coherent, raising the problem of choice between them; specifying what coherence amounts to precisely has proven difficult; Bayesian and probabilistic versions of coherence have been argued to face technical problems (the Bovens-Hartmann impossibility results); coherence is often a virtue without being sufficient for justification — observation, reliable processes, or other inputs seem to matter; Quine-style holism's prediction that any belief can be saved by adjusting other beliefs may be true in principle but practically rare; tension with non-doxastic states (perceptions, intuitions) that seem epistemically relevant.
primary_sources: Quine, W.V.O. (1951). 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism', Philosophical Review; BonJour, L. (1985). The Structure of Empirical Knowledge (foundational coherentist statement; subsequently abandoned); Bender, J.W. (ed.) (1989). The Current State of the Coherence Theory

name: Reliabilism
one_line_summary: Knowledge as belief produced by reliable cognitive processes.
extended_summary: Reliabilism is the epistemological position that knowledge consists of true belief produced by reliable cognitive processes — those that tend to produce true beliefs across relevantly similar situations. The position was substantially developed by Alvin Goldman in 'A Causal Theory of Knowing' (1967) and his subsequent work including Epistemology and Cognition (1986), with related contributions from Fred Dretske and David Armstrong. Reliabilism is the principal externalist alternative to internalist epistemologies (which hold that justification depends on factors accessible to the believer through reflection) — what makes a belief justified, on reliabilism, is the actual reliability of the process that produced it, regardless of whether the believer can articulate or even recognize that reliability. The framework has substantial appeal: it accommodates animal and infant knowledge (creatures whose belief-forming processes are reliable but who cannot reflect on them), perceptual knowledge (where reliability of perception matters even when we can't articulate why), and tacit expert knowledge. The principal challenge is the generality problem: any specific belief is produced by indefinitely many describable processes, and the reliability of those processes varies — what determines the relevant process? Goldman's later work and contemporary reliabilists have addressed this with substantial sophistication but no fully consensual solution. Reliabilism has substantial influence on naturalized epistemology and on virtue epistemology (where reliable cognitive processes are reframed as cognitive virtues).
originators: Alvin I. Goldman; Fred Dretske; David M. Armstrong; subsequent figures including Ernest Sosa, Linda Zagzebski
year_or_decade: 1967 (Goldman 'A Causal Theory of Knowing'); 1981 (Goldman 'What is Justified Belief?'); 1986 (Epistemology and Cognition)
core_components: Reliability of belief-forming process as criterion; Externalism (reliability need not be accessible to believer); Process reliability (truth-conduciveness across relevantly similar situations); Distinction from internalist alternatives (foundationalism, coherentism in their internalist variants); Accommodation of animal, infant, and tacit knowledge; Generality problem (which process is the relevant one?); Connection to virtue epistemology; Naturalized epistemology compatibility
primary_use_case: Foundational epistemological position in contemporary analytic philosophy; framework for thinking about knowledge in cases where the believer can't articulate justification; foundation for naturalized epistemology and virtue epistemology; resource for thinking about expert knowledge, perceptual knowledge, and animal cognition; influence on epistemology of testimony and social epistemology; basis for some arguments about the reliability of contested knowledge sources.
common_criticisms: Generality problem: any belief is produced by indefinitely many describable processes (perception, perception under specific lighting, perception by Tuesday afternoon, etc.) with different reliabilities — what determines the relevant process? No consensual solution; Bonjour's clairvoyance counterexamples: an agent reliably forming true beliefs through processes she has no awareness of seems not to have justified belief; new evil demon problem: a victim of systematic deception whose beliefs are unreliable through no fault of her own seems to be epistemically blameless, which reliabilism struggles to capture; the framework underweights the role of evidence and reasoning in epistemic justification; integration with broader epistemic concepts (understanding, wisdom) has been incomplete; some argue reliability is necessary but not sufficient for justification.
