primary_sources: Goldman, A.I. (1967). 'A Causal Theory of Knowing', Journal of Philosophy; Goldman, A.I. (1981). 'What is Justified Belief?', in Pappas (ed.) Justification and Knowledge; Goldman, A.I. (1986). Epistemology and Cognition

name: Occam's Razor
one_line_summary: Among competing hypotheses, prefer the one with fewest assumptions.
extended_summary: Occam's Razor is the methodological principle that among competing hypotheses adequate to explain a phenomenon, the one requiring the fewest assumptions or entities should be preferred. The principle is named for William of Ockham (c. 1287-1347), the English Franciscan philosopher and theologian whose works frequently invoked something like 'plurality must never be posited without necessity' and 'it is futile to do with more what can be done with fewer.' Ockham did not invent the principle (similar formulations appear in Aristotle, Maimonides, and Aquinas) but his vigorous methodological use earned the eponymy. The principle is preference rather than truth criterion — simpler hypotheses are not therefore more likely true, but they are preferred when both fit the evidence equally because they make fewer commitments and are easier to refute. Modern formal versions include statistical model selection criteria (AIC, BIC, Minimum Description Length) that mathematically formalize parsimony as a tradeoff against fit. The principle is widely cited but inconsistently applied — what counts as a 'simpler' hypothesis is itself contested, with simplicity measured variously as fewer entities, fewer parameters, more general principles, or shorter description. The principle is best understood as one heuristic among several rather than as an algorithm for hypothesis choice.
originators: William of Ockham (eponymous); precursors including Aristotle, Maimonides, Aquinas
year_or_decade: Early 14th century (Ockham); ancient and medieval precursors
core_components: Preference for fewer assumptions; 'Plurality must never be posited without necessity' (Ockham); 'Entities must not be multiplied beyond necessity' (later formulation, 'lex parsimoniae'); Heuristic rather than truth criterion; Modern formalizations: AIC (Akaike Information Criterion), BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion), Minimum Description Length; Connection to falsifiability (simpler theories are more easily refuted); Distinction from anti-realist 'eliminate entities' interpretation
primary_use_case: Scientific methodology and hypothesis selection; statistical model selection (AIC, BIC, MDL); pedagogical framework for distinguishing well-supported from over-elaborated explanations; widely-cited reasoning heuristic across disciplines; foundation for arguments against unnecessarily complex theoretical posits; reference in applied research design.
common_criticisms: What counts as 'simpler' is itself contested and depends on description language — a hypothesis that is simple in one framework may be complex in another; sometimes the more complex hypothesis is correct (biology has many entities and processes that elementary chemistry would have ruled out as superfluous); the principle's preference status is sometimes overstated as a truth criterion ('the simpler hypothesis is more likely true'), which is not the original meaning; in machine learning, simplicity as measured by parameter count interacts with overfitting concerns in ways that don't simply reduce to the original principle; popular use often deploys the razor as conversation-stopper rather than as one heuristic among several; Sober and others have argued the principle should be replaced by more rigorous Bayesian or information-theoretic considerations.
primary_sources: Ockham, W. (14th century). Various works including Summa Logicae, Sentences commentary; Sober, E. (2015). Ockham's Razors: A User's Manual

name: Hanlon's Razor
one_line_summary: Never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity.
extended_summary: Hanlon's Razor is the heuristic that one should not attribute to malice what can be adequately explained by stupidity, incompetence, or ignorance. The principle is conventionally attributed to Robert J. Hanlon based on a quip submitted to Arthur Bloch's Murphy's Law Book Two: More Reasons Why Things Go Wrong (1980), though similar formulations predate this — Robert Heinlein's 1941 novella 'Logic of Empire' contains nearly the same sentiment ('You have attributed conditions to villainy that simply result from stupidity'), Goethe's 1774 The Sorrows of Young Werther has a related line, and various aphoristic forms appear throughout history. The heuristic functions as a debiasing tool against the fundamental attribution error (overweighting personal/dispositional explanations for others' behavior) and against paranoid interpretations of mistakes, miscommunications, and accidents. It is widely cited in management, conflict resolution, and customer-service contexts. The principle's pop-culture form ('stupidity') has been increasingly softened in serious contexts to 'incompetence,' 'ignorance,' 'cognitive limitation,' or 'simpler explanation' — the underlying point is that benign explanations should be exhausted before invoking malice, not that the alternative is necessarily stupidity. The principle has obvious limits — sometimes malice is the right explanation, and Hanlon's Razor can rationalize ignoring genuine bad-faith behavior.
originators: Robert J. Hanlon (eponymous, 1980); Robert Heinlein (1941 precursor); broader aphoristic tradition
year_or_decade: 1980 (Hanlon's submission to Murphy's Law Book Two); 1941 (Heinlein precursor)
core_components: Preference for benign over malicious explanation; Debiasing against fundamental attribution error; Heuristic, not truth criterion; Softer modern formulations ('incompetence,' 'ignorance,' 'simpler explanation'); Connection to Occam's Razor (benign explanations often simpler than conspiracy); Limits when genuine malice is operating
primary_use_case: Management and team conflict; customer service and stakeholder relationships; debiasing tool in interpersonal interpretation; heuristic for avoiding paranoid escalation in workplace and political contexts; pedagogical reference for teaching about attribution biases.
common_criticisms: Sometimes malice is the right explanation, and the razor can rationalize ignoring genuine bad-faith behavior — particularly problematic in patterns of harassment, discrimination, or fraud where the principle becomes a tool for excusing harmful actors; the principle's framing assumes stupidity is the alternative, when many of the actual alternatives (cognitive limitation, divergent values, structural pressures, cultural difference) are quite different from stupidity; can become a rhetorical move to dismiss legitimate concerns ('don't be paranoid'); attribution to 'stupidity' is itself sometimes more insulting than attribution to malice and may not be the cooperative move it presents itself as; the principle works as one heuristic among several, not as algorithm; doesn't address structural or institutional sources of harm that are neither personal malice nor personal stupidity.
primary_sources: Bloch, A. (1980). Murphy's Law Book Two: More Reasons Why Things Go Wrong (Hanlon's submission); Heinlein, R.A. (1941). 'Logic of Empire'

name: Sturgeon's Law
one_line_summary: Ninety percent of everything is crud — used to push past surface dismissal.
extended_summary: Sturgeon's Law (or Sturgeon's Revelation) was articulated by science-fiction writer Theodore Sturgeon in defense of his genre against critics who dismissed it on the basis of weak examples. Sturgeon's response, presented at a 1951 World Science Fiction Convention and elaborated in print thereafter, was that 'ninety percent of everything is crud' — and that judging any genre, field, or category by its worst examples is unfair because the same is true of literary fiction, classical music, philosophical writing, or any other category. The fair test is to compare the best of any category against the best of others, not the average against the average. The principle is now widely cited beyond science fiction as a heuristic for evaluating fields, genres, methodologies, and bodies of work — the exhortation to engage with the strongest representatives rather than dismissing on the basis of bad examples. The 'ninety percent' figure is approximate and somewhat arbitrary; the underlying point is that mediocre examples are the norm in any sufficiently large category, and selection effects (which examples are sampled, what counts as 'representative') drive most apparent differences in quality between fields. The principle is a useful complement to steelmanning, both encouraging engagement with strong rather than weak versions of a position or field.
originators: Theodore Sturgeon
year_or_decade: 1951 (WorldCon talk); 1957 (published as 'On Hand: A Book' in Venture Science Fiction, March 1958)
core_components: Ninety percent of any field is mediocre or worse; Fair comparison requires best-vs-best, not average-vs-average; Heuristic against dismissing fields by their weakest examples; Connection to selection effects in sampling representative work; Complement to steelmanning; Application across genres, fields, methodologies
primary_use_case: Heuristic for fair evaluation of fields, genres, and bodies of work; debiasing against dismissive sampling; intellectual-honesty practice in cross-disciplinary engagement; complement to steelmanning in argument; reference in intellectual-culture discussions about fields, genres, and methodologies; pedagogical tool for teaching fair evaluation.
common_criticisms: The specific 'ninety percent' figure is approximate and not empirically grounded; what counts as 'crud' is contested and value-laden; the principle can be deployed to deflect legitimate criticism of a field as a whole when its problems are systemic rather than individual-quality variation; some fields' best examples may genuinely be substantially worse than other fields' best examples — the principle doesn't preclude legitimate cross-field quality comparison; like other 'razors,' Sturgeon's Law is a heuristic that doesn't substitute for substantive engagement; can become a rhetorical move ('you're judging us by our weakest examples') without actual best-of-field engagement.
primary_sources: Sturgeon, T. (1958). 'On Hand: A Book', Venture Science Fiction (March 1958)

name: Steelmanning
one_line_summary: Construct the strongest possible version of an opposing argument before engaging it.
extended_summary: Steelmanning is the rhetorical and intellectual practice of constructing the strongest possible version of an opposing argument before engaging it — the deliberate inverse of strawmanning (engaging with a weakened or distorted version of an opposing position). The term emerged in rationalist communities (particularly LessWrong, where it was popularized by Eliezer Yudkowsky and others) in the late 2000s and early 2010s, building on much older intellectual traditions of charitable interpretation including the Talmudic principle of debating the strongest version of opposing arguments, John Stuart Mill's emphasis in On Liberty (1859) on engaging the best version of competing views ('he who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that'), and the principle of charity in philosophy (Davidson, Quine — interpret others' utterances so as to maximize their truth or rationality). The practice is closely related to Sturgeon's Law (engage with the best examples), but distinct: Sturgeon addresses sampling across a field, while steelmanning addresses argument-by-argument engagement. Effective steelmanning requires genuine effort to understand and improve the opposing position — even articulating it more compellingly than its actual proponents have — before engaging. The practice has obvious epistemic and ethical virtues but also limits: when the strongest version of an argument is genuinely much stronger than what proponents actually argue, steelmanning can become an exercise in straw-manning the proponents while engaging an artifact of one's own construction.
originators: LessWrong rationalist community popularization (2000s-2010s); Eliezer Yudkowsky; older intellectual traditions including Mill, Talmudic argument, principle of charity
year_or_decade: 2010s LessWrong popularization; older intellectual traditions
core_components: Construct strongest version of opposing argument; Inverse of strawmanning; Connection to principle of charity (Davidson, Quine); Mill's argument in On Liberty for engaging best opposing views; Distinction from Sturgeon's Law (argument-level vs field-level); Limits when steelman differs substantially from actual proponents' position; Genuine effort to improve opposing position; Pre-engagement step in serious argument
primary_use_case: Intellectual practice in serious argument; debiasing tool against motivated reasoning; rationalist-community methodology; teaching tool for substantive engagement; complement to strong-style philosophy and analytic argument; basis for many practices around productive disagreement; reference in contemporary online intellectual culture.
common_criticisms: When the strongest version of an argument is substantially stronger than what proponents actually argue, steelmanning can become engagement with an artifact rather than with the actual position — and proponents may legitimately object that the steelman is not their argument; effort required for genuine steelmanning is high and most casual deployment of the term is closer to weak charity; ironymanning (constructing a position so reasonable it resembles the opponent's actual position less than a charitable representation) is a known failure mode; in some cases the actual weakness of an argument is the point — steelmanning weak arguments may misrepresent the field of opposition; can become a rhetorical move signaling intellectual virtue without actually engaging with what the opponent is saying; tension with respecting opponents' actual stated views; the term itself has been argued to be needlessly martial.
primary_sources: Yudkowsky, E. and LessWrong community (2010s onward). Various posts at lesswrong.com; Mill, J.S. (1859). On Liberty (chapter 2 antecedent); Davidson, D. (1973). 'Radical Interpretation' (principle of charity)
